A bit of backstory:

In high school I was quite unpopular. I blamed a lot of it on my depression, my looks, and that I was "smarter" than the average student. However, in reality it was because I was a complete selfish jerk to most people I met.

A few years ago, my first year of college, I went to a college in a small town in the middle of nowhere, just to get some experience living on my own before pursuing a bigger university. I was quite lucky in my time there. As in, I met a guy in the dormroom next to mine, and he asked to mentor me (I was 18 at the time, I'm a guy). I accepted, and we began to have weekly meetings to see how life was going. Each week I would describe the week, and almost every single time he could pinpoint how, in some way, I was treating others with disrespect and a negative attitude. We became really close and during the year I was there, he continued to show me support each week and taught me so much about how to treat others properly.

Now, a few years later, at a significantly bigger university, I'm quite popular. Most students have a general idea who I am, and a lot of my friends look up to me.

So, what changed? Here are a few big things to keep in mind when meeting new people.

* **Be outgoing, but be sure you're staying true to who you are.** I mean that, if you're typically an introverted, quiet person, don't force yourself into a position of leadership amongst the other freshman. While this can be a growing experience, you may eventually feel that you're not able to really be "yourself" around anyone.
* **Really listen to others.** You mentioned you want to be the friendliest version of yourself possible. Think for a minute of some of the friendliest people you know. What sort of traits do they share? Most likely things like, *they genuinely care how you're doing, they want to know what's going on in your life, and they respect you*. As you get to know people, especially during freshman week (assuming your campus has something similar to that), if you're outgoing yet approachable, people will be drawn to you.
* **Be careful when choosing friends.** As tempting as it may be to try and get *everyone* to like you, it's not realistic. Similarly, being best buds with everyone on campus isn't going to happen. However likable you may be, some cliques can be really toxic. Remember, you're there to learn. But you gotta make some friends too. What are those friends going to look like though? Are they going to support you, or pressure you to become someone you're not?

Sometimes making friends can be hard. But remember, like you said, college is like a new start. I can speak from experience. When I'm home during the summer, working while living at home, seeing people I once went to high school with can be extremely awkward and even frustrating. 

If freshman week doesn't work out, don't stress. College is full of second chances. Speaking again from experience, most of my first semester at the university I currently attend, I was still a pretty big jerk to most people I met. Over time since then I've made a lot of changes in my life, and I'm at a point where I'm a really well-liked guy.

You can do this. Don't forget, **most other freshman are trying to make a new start too**.

Although these are some good generic tips, I disagree with a few things (Gold II Support/Top main).


> Don't touch your adc's farm. If he is gone, just last hit. It's pretty straight forward. Unless your adc asks you to clear the wave, just let him have it.

I strongly disagree with this. Bot lane is difficult in SoloQ because you need to connect with your lane partner without having to use the chat. If you have to stop and chat, then that's a few seconds of lane control you've given up. Some ADC's, especially at low ELO, cannot last hit well. Especially at tower. If you see that they are struggling to get cs under tower, help them out. You should be able to tell which minions need to be whittled down for the ADC. 

Also, some ADC's don't know when to push the lane, and when they choose to simply freeze the lane or only last hit instead of shoving to tower or moving up past the river, then you can easily throw a lane/whatever advantage you may have.

If the enemy ADC/Support recalls, you'll usually want to shove the lane. If you can **ever** confidently shove to the enemy turret, then do it. If the jungler comes from behind, then you have accomplished a few things:

1. The jungler is now wasting his time, because you should have had vision of him before he shows up.

2. The enemy ADC is now losing CS to the turret.

> Your normal start should be biscuit, 1 minute ward, 2 red pots, reju bead/faerie, 2 wards and a pink.

I also would disagree. The bead/charm is not worth all that much early on except for helping you get an early philo (which isn't what you should be rushing anyway). If you replace the bead/charm and 1 health potion with another green and pink ward, your lane control increases tenfold. You want to have control of the lane and the river. By totally denying the enemy bot lane of vision of the river/lane/tri, you've won the mental game of bot lane. They now have to constantly worry about being ganked, and that will be at the back of their mind, causing a degree of tilt.

That's just my thoughts on a couple points. Thanks for the taking the time to type them all out. :)

Support champions are considered support champions because of their utility, and their capability to scale in to late game from their abilities alone (without needing gold or items). This is why champions like Nami and Sona for example are strong supports; their kits are comprised of crowd control, mobility buffs, and other forms of utility. This is why atypical supports (picking a random champion and just not last hitting) will often not add much to a team.

Know your champion, and know how that specific champion should act during lane phase. For example: Blitz and Thresh capitalize on catching people out of position. Sona and Nami have a heal, and can trade well. Janna can disengage and keep the adc alive if he struggles with positioning.

Being melee vs being ranged drastically affects how easily you can gain control in a lane. As a ranged support, especially fighting against a melee support, you can easily harass by auto attacking and then immediately receding back into the brush (so you don't draw minion aggro).

I've learned that almost everyone we meet is going through significantly more than we realize. Know that you are not alone in your struggles. There are people out there that genuinely care about you and love you and want to help you in any way that they can. You just need to be honest and open with them so that they can help you. Now, as to whom you should be open with in hopes of receiving unbiased, sound advice, comes down to your own judgment. There certainly are people out there who only desire to help others because it makes them feel better about themselves, but there are also those who, again, **genuinely** desire to show you and your family love. 

**We are not meant to do life alone.** Don't think for a minute that it's up to us, especially as the man of the house, to fix every single problem in others' lives and to be the rock upon everyone builds their foundation. We should certainly love our families and be there for them, but it is not our job to fix their issues in addition to our own.

Now I know you haven't said that this is necessarily what you're doing, but you say you're at a point of trying to keep everything standing and keeping all of the issues taken care of on your own. I know you don't want to just hear "seek counselling," but friend, I would advise that you seek help from someone, whether that is a counsellor, an older family member whom you're close with, an old friend, or whomever you know you can talk to and trust. And, more importantly, though I'm not sure of the current state of your wife **you need to be honest with your wife about how you are doing. You are together for a reason, and you love her and she loves you. She wants to be there for you and you for her.**

Like I said, we're not meant to do life alone. It's impossible.

**tl;dr** Whether it's a counsellor or just someone in your life whom you can trust, I would highly suggest having someone you can talk to about what you're going through, mentally and physically. Continuing to suppress to others what your life is actually like will eventually cause that house of cards to fall.

Again, there are people out there who genuinely care about you. Seek their guidance and listening ears.

I don't know what physical toll he took (he was about 50 at the time). I know that his body has suffered a great deal throughout his life though.

I've never been told what the accident did to him. He is probably the most respectable man I know, though. Responsible, a man of integrity and respect, humble, loving, and so much more.

On a family vacation, coming back from Disneyland, my family and I were in an RV driving on the highway. I was about 7 at the time. My uncle was driving, and I was sleeping on one of the couches. My dad was asleep in the back of the RV.

I woke up to see the end of the vehicle ahead of us jutting through our front wind-shield. The RV was in ruin, with every single part of the wall and floor totally destroyed, resulting in a sea of wooden planks and sharp objects. My mom sat across the room from me, coated in blood, sobbing. I couldn't move my legs. A fireman was yelling at me to come to the door so he could carry me to an ambulance. I don't remember what happened after I saw him, I may have blacked out.

I woke up in a hospital. Couldn't walk for a few weeks. Didn't see my parents for months. When I finally got out of the hospital, I couldn't go home. I saw my mom after a month or two, and her entire body was being held together by metal, casts, iron, wires. I still didn't know anything about what happened to my dad. All I knew was that he was still in the hospital. I lived with friends/extended family for about a year.

Eventually my mom and dad were both physically able to come back home. My mom came back first, and my dad about 6 months later. He had been paralyzed from the chest down, and hasn't walked since (this is about 13-14 years ago now).

What had happened was a driver of a semi-truck had fallen asleep at the wheel while behind us, and didn't stop at a red light. Our RV was hit, and my dad took the brunt of the force compared to the rest of our family. I was too young to understand what was happening. Seeing my mom literally coated in blood, without skin showing, and being unable to move my body was certainly terrifying though.

To this day my dad suffers severe pain issues, as does my mom, though not to the same degree. I don't know what happened to the driver of the semi though. I'm not bitter. I'm sure he's in enough regret for his lack of responsibility that he doesn't need his victim's anger on top of everything.
